newsitem.title: USA: High-yield debt volume concern as cycle ages -S&P.
newsitem.headline: High-yield debt volume concern as cycle ages -S&P.

text.p: A precipitous rise in high-yield debt issuance in 1996 is "a bit of a concern" for Standard & Poor's in 1997 considering an imminent downturn in the current economic cycle, said Leo O'Neill, president and chief ratings officer on Monday.
O'Neill stressed an economic downturn is probably not in the offing for the near-term, but some fade is inevitable as the economy enters the sixth-year of economic expansion.
"The ability of investors to be repaid on time is increasingly reliant on economic conditions," O'Neill said.
Despite the fact high-yield credits are better analysed now than in the late 1980s, O'Neill said that won't prevent them feeling pressure from cyclical troughs.
Asked about contentions that high-yields can weather hard times better now than they could in previous years, he said: "I don't buy it."

He noted issuance in the single-B tier of the high-yield market doubled in 1996 to about $40 billion in 1996. Issuance of all high-yield credits, which comprises about 60 percent of the total corporate bond market, rose 66 percent in 1996.

High-yields have lured investors anxious for higher returns in an environment of relatively low interest rates, he said, while a lot of the securities end up in high-yield bond funds which to some extent masks their risks.
In another sign of the economy's support of credit quality, only 14 rated corporate issuers defaulted in 1996 representing 44 percent of defaults in 1995, he said.

Broadly speaking, O'Neill said corporate debt issuers that enjoyed a broadly favorable credit rating environment in 1996 should work to preserve their status in 1997 ahead of an imminent economic slowdown.

O'Neill said global credit quality improved in 1996 with upgrades far exceeding downgrades in terms of dollar volume. Downgrades of industrial and telecommunications issuers actually outnumbered upgrades based on the number of issuers, however.
The global credit picture is positive, he said, but all sectors are reaping benefits.
Rating outlooks for 1997 are sanguine for energy, transportation, capital goods, high-technology and healthcare sectors, O'Neill said.
Sectors with a negative spin include insurance companies (property/casualty and life/health), metals and mining, telecommunications, consumer products and media and entertainment, he said.

O'Neill also stressed the importance of international and sovereign markets in the coming years. In 1996, S&P raised the ratings on $8.57 billion in debt from seven sovereign issuers and downgraded only two representing $1.46 billion.
"This proliferation of sovereign ratings is a sign that governments are increasingly utilizing ratings to gain access to capital at favorable terms in cross-border public markets," O'Neill said.

Credit improvements in the U.S. public finance sector were broad-based with most sectors sharing in a record 672 upgrades for 1996. By contrast, public finance issuers finished the year with 190 downgrades.

Municipal electric utilities accounted for 84 percent of the total downgraded debt, S&P said. Looking ahead, utilities will have to curtail costs and adjust their rate structures to meet new challenges presented by pending competition and deregulation, S&P said.
